analysis.one_liner: Bans importing foreign-made semiautomatic assault rifles, pistols, and large-capacity ammunition magazines.
analysis.headline: The bill died in the Senate Finance Committee without a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor.
analysis.plain_summary: Senator Daniel Patrick Moynihan proposed prohibiting the importation of semiautomatic assault rifles and pistols, ammunition magazines holding more than five rounds, and accessories like grenade launchers, flash suppressors, and bayonets. The ban applied only to imported weapons; guns and magazines made in the United States would remain legal. Government agencies were exempted. The bill was sent to the Senate Finance Committee, which handles import restrictions, and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: If passed, the main beneficiary would be the general public through reduced availability of imported military-style rifles and pistols and imported high-capacity magazines. Domestic gun manufacturers would also gain a protected market, since foreign competition would be cut off while their own production remained unrestricted.
analysis.who_benefits_short: The general public; also domestic gun makers

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits importing semiautomatic assault rifles and pistols from a named list including AK-47, Uzi, HK91, and FAL types, plus any others the President designates.
Bans imported detachable magazines, belts, and drums holding more than five rounds, including kits from which such devices can be assembled.
Bans imported accessories such as grenade launchers, bayonets, flash suppressors, night sights, and silencer adapters designed for semiautomatic weapons.
The CRS summary confirms the bill prohibits importation of assault weapons, large-capacity feeding devices, and accessories, with specified exceptions.

analysis.who_pays: Foreign firearm manufacturers and American importers and dealers of foreign-made rifles would lose access to the US market, and American buyers of those models would lose legal access. Because the ban covers imports only, it imposes no restriction on domestic manufacturers or on sales of US-made weapons.

drawbacks.text: The bill covers imports only: identical rifles, pistols, and high-capacity magazines manufactured in the United States would remain fully legal, limiting any public-safety benefit.

The five-round magazine threshold is stricter than the ten-round standard later used in federal law, which critics would call burdensome for owners of popular imported sporting rifles like the HK91 and FAL listed in the bill.
Importation by federal, state, and local government agencies is exempted, so the ban affects only civilian access.
The bill leaves enforcement and the open-ended power to add weapon types to the President, which critics could argue gives one office too much discretion over what becomes contraband.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public-safety gain is real but narrow: it would have cut off foreign-made assault weapons and high-capacity magazines while leaving the domestic market untouched, so the supply of the same weapons could continue from US factories. The cost falls on importers and buyers of specific foreign models, some of which are ordinary sporting rifles. As designed, the bill attacks a problem at only one of its two sources.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, which never acted on it, and it expired when the Congress ended in January 1993.

narrative.text: Senator Moynihan introduced the bill on April 9, 1991.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance, which handles import and tariff matters.
The action history shows no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action for the rest of the 102nd Congress.
The bill never received a vote and died when the Congress ended on January 3, 1993.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Importers and dealers of foreign-made semiautomatic rifles and magazines are better off, since imports remained unrestricted, and domestic manufacturers are better off because no restriction on their sales advanced.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Foreign gun importers and domestic makers

for.name: Sen. Daniel Patrick Moynihan
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to committee; it drew no cosponsors.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. Lloyd Bentsen (D-TX)
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill: no hearing, no markup, no vote, and no report during the two-plus years before the Congress ended.

against.name: National Rifle Association
against.what_they_did: Opposed restrictions on semiautomatic firearms and magazine capacity during this period; no NRA action on this bill appears in the congressional record.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and no other senator cosponsored, so the partisan shape of support and opposition is unknown from the record.

industries.industry: Foreign firearm manufacturers and US importers
industries.note: The bill would have cut off their US market for semi-automatic rifles, pistols, and large-capacity magazines. Their interest in continuing imports ran against the bill's public-safety goal.

An import ban would have removed foreign competition for the same weapons while leaving domestic production and sales fully legal, locking in the domestic industry's share of the semi-automatic rifle market. Their interest in unrestricted sales of the same weapons ran against the bill's stated purpose.
